title: Pull & Fetch
subtitle: Get updates from the remote into your local repo
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Your teammates pushed new commits. Your local repo is behind. You need their changes to continue working without creating conflicts.
whyItExists.solution: git fetch downloads new commits from the remote without changing your working files. git pull fetches AND merges (or rebases) — it's the most common way to update your local branch.
whyItExists.whenToUse: At the start of every work session: git pull. Before creating a PR: git pull to make sure you're current. Before pushing: git fetch to check if anyone beat you to it.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't pull in the middle of uncommitted work — stash first. Don't pull --rebase on main if your team uses merge commits.

explainModes.beginner: git pull downloads teammates' commits and adds them to your branch. git fetch only downloads but doesn't change your files — you decide what to do with them after.
explainModes.simple: git pull = git fetch + git merge. Fetches new commits from origin and merges them into your current branch. git fetch downloads updates to origin/main but doesn't touch your local main — safe to inspect first.
explainModes.standard: git pull --rebase replays your local commits on top of the remote's commits (instead of creating a merge commit). Cleaner history. git fetch + git log origin/main to see what changed before merging. After fetch: git merge origin/main or git rebase origin/main manually.
explainModes.technical: git fetch updates remote tracking branches (origin/main etc.) — read-only snapshots of the remote's state. git pull <remote> <branch> fetches and then merges the remote tracking branch into your current branch. pull.rebase = true in config makes git pull use rebase by default. FETCH_HEAD stores the fetched commits temporarily.
explainModes.deepDive: git pull uses the configured remote and tracking branch for the current branch (set by -u on push). git fetch --prune removes remote tracking branches for remote branches that were deleted. git fetch --all fetches all remotes. A pull with conflicts leaves the repo in a 'merging' state — resolve the conflicts, git add, git merge --continue. shallow repos (--depth 1) can't fetch older commits without git fetch --unshallow.

content.code:
# Download updates without changing your files
git fetch origin

# See what's new on the remote
git log origin/main --oneline
# or
git log HEAD..origin/main --oneline   # commits on remote but not local

# After inspecting, merge manually
git merge origin/main

# Fetch all remotes
git fetch --all

# Fetch and prune deleted remote branches
git fetch --prune

# Standard pull (fetch + merge)
git pull

# Pull from specific remote and branch
git pull origin main

# Pull with rebase instead of merge (cleaner history)
git pull --rebase

# Set rebase as default pull behaviour
git config --global pull.rebase true

# Start of day workflow
git switch main
git pull
git switch feature/my-task
git rebase main   # bring in the latest main into your feature branch

questions.question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
options: fetch is faster; pull is for large repos
fetch downloads commits but doesn't change your working files; pull fetches AND merges
fetch only works with SSH; pull works with HTTPS
questions.explanation: git fetch downloads new commits to the remote tracking branch (origin/main) but leaves your local branch untouched. git pull does fetch + merge in one step. Fetch lets you inspect before merging; pull is quicker for everyday use.

faq.q: Should I use git pull or git fetch + git merge?
faq.a: Both are fine. git pull is simpler for daily use. git fetch + inspect + merge gives you more control — you can see what changed before integrating. Use git pull --rebase to get a cleaner linear history.

faq.q: git pull failed with 'Not possible to fast-forward'. What now?
faq.a: Both your local branch and the remote have new commits. Either merge: git pull (creates a merge commit), or rebase: git pull --rebase (replays your commits on top). If you see many of these, consider making git pull always rebase: git config --global pull.rebase true.

examples: git pull is arguably the most-run git command in team workflows
git fetch --prune cleans up remote tracking branches for deleted remote branches
Pair programming: both devs git pull before switching who's driving
